title: What If Millions of Spiders Fled a Flood at Once? An Australian Town Woke Up Under Silk

scenes.text: What if every spider in a valley fled a flood at once? Australia found out in 2012.
March 2012, Wagga Wagga, New South Wales. The Murrumbidgee River peaks above 10 meters, and thousands of people are evacuated.
Spiders cannot evacuate. As the water rises, millions climb anything standing and fire strands of silk into the wind.
The strands catch the breeze and lift the spiders away. It is called ballooning, and when millions do it at once the silk lands everywhere.
Within days, fields, fences and whole paddocks are wrapped in white sheets of web, like snow. Walk through and it clings to your legs.
The spiders were mostly tiny sheet weavers, harmless to people. The flood retreats, the silk blows away, and the spiders ride back down to start again.

description:
What if millions of spiders fled a flood at once? In March 2012 the Murrumbidgee River at Wagga Wagga, New South Wales peaked above 10 metres and thousands of residents were evacuated. As the water rose, spiders climbed onto fences, posts and plants and released silk threads to be carried off by the wind, a dispersal behaviour called ballooning.
With so many spiders ballooning at once, the silk blanketed fields and paddocks around the town in white sheets. The Australian Museum identified most of the spiders as small sheet weavers of the family Linyphiidae, up to about a centimetre long and harmless to people; photographs also showed wolf spiders. The same thing happens after floods wherever spiders need to escape the water.

first_comment: Spiders balloon every year to spread out; a flood just forces millions to do it on the same day, which is why the silk piles up like snow. What should we run through next: what if spiders were the size of dogs? Drop your own what-if below.
